intro: Gwytherin is a small village in the hills of Conwy in north Wales, a few miles south of Llangernyw and its famous yew. In the churchyard of St Winifred's, two old yews stand either side of the path to the church, their crowns almost meeting overhead, and a row of four standing stones keeps them company. A reader photographed them and sent them to us; they put the yews at more than 2,000 years old.

trees.story:
Two yews stand either side of the path into the churchyard at Gwytherin, a small village in the hills of Conwy, and a reader who walked between them in November 2026 sent us their photographs.

"Two ancient yew trees in the churchyard of St Winifred's," they wrote, and they put the pair at more than 2,000 years old. That is their estimate, not a measurement we have seen. Churchyard yews are famously hard to date, because an old trunk goes hollow and loses the rings that would tell.

What the pictures show needs no figure. The two crowns rise dark and wide over rows of slate headstones, almost meeting above the path, so that you walk up to the church through the gap between them. Up close the trunks are red-brown and fluted into deep vertical ropes, the wood twisting round the base as if it had been poured and left to set.

The reader also pointed out a row of four standing stones in the same churchyard, along the side of the church.

Walk the path between the two yews, then go slowly round each trunk in turn.

question_meta: The Gwytherin yews in Conwy, north Wales: where the two churchyard yews stand, how to find them, and what we still want to know.
question_answer: The Gwytherin Yews are two old yews either side of the path through the churchyard of St Winifred's in Gwytherin, a village in the hills of Conwy, north Wales. The churchyard is free to visit.
question_context: A reader sent us photographs of these two yews from the churchyard of St Winifred's at Gwytherin, a small village in the hills of Conwy in north Wales. The trees stand either side of the path up to the church, their dark crowns almost meeting overhead, with rows of slate headstones in the grass around them. Close to, both trunks are red-brown and deeply fluted, the bark running in thick vertical ropes and twisting at the base. The reader puts the pair at more than 2,000 years old. That is their estimate; we have no measured girth or written source for the age, and churchyard yews are hard to date because an old trunk goes hollow and loses its rings. The same churchyard holds a row of four standing stones along the side of the church, which the reader also pointed out. Gwytherin lies a few miles south of Llangernyw, whose churchyard yew is one of the best known in Wales, so the two villages make a short tour of old yews. Readers who have measured the Gwytherin trunks can add their figures on the tree's page.
